draft.title: Appeals
card: An appeal asks a higher court to review a decision made by a lower court. It is not a new trial from the start.
either side can appeal against a sentence. The accused may argue it is too harsh. The Crown (the prosecution) may argue it is too lenient.
only the accused can appeal against a conviction, which is a finding of guilt. The accused argues the finding of guilt was wrong.
The appeal goes to a higher court than the one that made the decision. For example, a Local Court decision can go to the District Court.
draft.remember: An appeal sends a decision to a higher court. The accused can challenge a conviction or sentence, and the Crown can challenge a sentence.

a.q: Which appeal is open to the Crown after an accused person is sentenced?
opts: An appeal arguing the sentence is too lenient
An appeal arguing the conviction was wrong
An appeal to the same court that sentenced
An appeal arguing the sentence is too harsh
a.why: The Crown can appeal against a sentence, and it does so when it thinks the sentence is too lenient. Arguing that a sentence is too harsh is the accused's argument, and a conviction appeal belongs to the accused only.
a.clue: The Crown is the prosecution, so which result would it dislike?

b.q: Tariq is found guilty of fraud in the Local Court and given a sentence he accepts. He now believes the court was wrong to find him guilty. What can he do?
opts: Appeal against the conviction to a higher court
Appeal only against the sentence to a higher court
Ask the Crown to appeal the conviction for him
Do nothing, because an accepted sentence ends all appeals
b.why: The accused can appeal against a conviction, whatever view he takes of the sentence. Accepting the sentence does not stop him challenging the finding of guilt. Appealing only against the sentence would not address his complaint, which is about guilt.
b.clue: His complaint is about the finding of guilt, not the penalty.

a.best: An appeal arguing the sentence is too lenient

b.best: Appeal against the conviction to a higher court
